content: Insulin glargine is a synthetic, long-acting form of human insulin used to manage blood sugar levels in individuals with type 1 diabetes, where the body does not produce insulin, and in individuals with type 2 diabetes who require long-acting insulin to control their condition. Insulin is a hormone produced by the pancreas that facilitates the movement of glucose from the bloodstream into tissues for energy use and helps metabolize carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. In diabetes, the pancreas does not produce sufficient insulin, necessitating external supplementation. Without proper management, diabetes can lead to complications such as nerve damage, blood vessel issues, kidney disease, and vision problems. Insulin glargine is administered as a subcutaneous injection (under the skin, not into a vein) once daily, typically at bedtime. It is available in vials or prefilled cartridges. The required dose depends on factors such as diet, exercise, other medical conditions, and concurrent medications, and it may change over time. It is crucial to follow your doctor’s instructions precisely and not to alter the dose or frequency without medical advice. Insulin glargine helps control diabetes but does not cure it, so it must be taken consistently, even if you feel well. Do not stop using it without consulting your doctor. The medication should not be shaken, diluted, or mixed with other insulins or solutions. If using cartridges, they are compatible only with the OptiPen One Insulin Delivery Device. Before first use, carefully read the instructions provided and have a healthcare provider demonstrate the correct technique. If using vials, the insulin must be drawn into a syringe. Disposable syringes should be used once and never shared to avoid infection or incorrect dosing. If it appears cloudy or contains particles, discard it. For a new vial, remove the protective cap but not the rubber stopper, and clean the stopper with alcohol. Inject air into the vial equal to the required dose, then withdraw the insulin while ensuring no air bubbles remain in the syringe. If bubbles are present, tap the syringe to release them and adjust the dose as needed. Use a new syringe for each injection. For injection, choose a site such as the abdomen, thighs, buttocks, or arms. Clean the area with alcohol, pinch the skin, and insert the needle at a 45to 90-degree angle. Inject the insulin slowly, leave the needle in place for a few seconds, then remove it and press lightly on the site without rubbing. Rotate injection sites within the same general area to avoid using the same spot more than once a month. Dispose of needles and syringes as instructed. Before starting insulin glargine, inform your doctor of any allergies, current medications (including over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and herbal products), and any history of thyroid, liver, or kidney disease. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you experience fever, infection, injury, or gastrointestinal illness, inform your doctor, as these conditions may affect your blood sugar levels. Additionally, disclose your use of insulin glargine to any healthcare provider before surgery, including dental procedures. Follow your doctor’s dietary and exercise recommendations. Do not begin a new diet or exercise regimen without consulting your doctor, as your insulin dose may need adjustment. Alcohol can lower blood sugar levels, so discuss safe consumption with your doctor. If you miss a dose or accidentally take an extra dose, consult your doctor for specific instructions. Write these directions down for future reference. Insulin glargine may cause changes in blood sugar levels. Be aware of the symptoms of hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), such as shakiness, dizziness, sweating, irritability, headache, numbness around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, hunger, or clumsy movements. Severe hypoglycemia can lead to confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness, requiring immediate medical attention. Symptoms of hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) include extreme thirst, frequent urination, hunger, weakness, and blurred vision. Untreated hyperglycemia can result in diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening condition characterized by dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, fruity-smelling breath, and decreased consciousness. Contact your doctor immediately if you experience these symptoms. Common side effects of insulin glargine include redness, swelling, pain, or itching at the injection site, as well as changes in skin texture, such as thickening or dimpling. Severe side effects, such as widespread rash, difficulty breathing, swelling, or a rapid pulse, require immediate medical attention. Store unopened insulin glargine in the refrigerator, but do not freeze it. If refrigeration is unavailable, store it at room temperature away from heat and sunlight. Unrefrigerated vials or cartridges must be used within 14–28 days, depending on the product, or discarded. Once a cartridge is placed in the OptiPen One device, do not refrigerate it. Dispose of expired or unused insulin properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance. In case of overdose, contact a poison control center or emergency services immediately. Keep all medical appointments and monitor your blood sugar and HbA1c levels as directed. Inform your doctor of any changes in weight, diet, exercise, or emotional stress, as these may require dose adjustments. Wear medical alert identification indicating you have diabetes, and carry extra insulin and supplies when traveling. Maintain good hygiene and promptly treat any wounds to prevent infection. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist with any questions about refills. Insulin glargine is marketed under the brand name Lantus®.
